beats.script_body: The Western world's first and largest museum dedicated to Himalayan culture holds more than 2,000 items, dating from the second to the twentieth centuries, from the mountainous regions between Afghanistan and Myanmar. A steel-and-marble spiral staircase winds up through the seven-story building to galleries of Buddhist sculptures, vibrant Tibetan thangkas, or scroll paintings, ornate geometric mandalas, carved masks, and woven textiles. On the third floor, the rotating "Masterworks: Jewels of the Collection" showcases highlights such as a fourteenth-century Nepali Buddha and a Tibetan bronze of a divine couple.

physical_cues.cue: Steel-and-marble spiral staircase winding up through the seven-story building

beats.source_passage: The Western world's first and largest museum dedicated to Himalayan culture holds more than 2,000 items. They include pieces dating from the second to the 20th centuries from the mountainous regions between Afghanistan and Myanmar (Burma). A steel-and-marble spiral staircase winds up through the sevenstory building to galleries that display Buddhist sculptures, vibrant Tibetan thangkas (scroll paintings), ornate geometric paintings called mandalas, carved masks, and skillfully woven textiles. On the third floor, the regularly rotating exhibit "Masterworks: Jewels of the Collection" showcases outstanding works of art, such as a 14th-century Nepali Buddha; a Tibetan bronze of a divine couple, "Samvara in Union with Vajrayogini".

beats.script_body: During the 1950s and '60s, the Chelsea Hotel became a bohemian commune where artists, musicians, and writers hung out. The famed venue played host to musical luminaries including Bob Dylan, Patti Smith, Jimi Hendrix, and Janis Joplin, as well as writers such as Arthur Miller and Gore Vidal. Songs, stories, and novels were written both in and about the hotel — Arthur C. Clarke penned 2001: A Space Odyssey while staying here.

beats.source_passage: During the 1950s and '60s, artists, musicians, and writers hung out at the Chelsea Hotel (popularly known as Hotel Chelsea) in what had become a bohemian commune. The famed venue has played host to such musical luminaries as Bob Dylan, Patti Smith, Jimi Hendrix, and Janis Joplin, as well as many writers—Arthur Miller and Gore Vidal among them. Songs, stories, and novels have been written both in and about the hotel, including 2001: A Space Odyssey, which Arthur C. Clarke penned while staying here.

beats.script_body: The hotel saw its share of tragedy. It was here that years of heavy drinking caught up with the Welsh poet Dylan Thomas, who died after collapsing at the hotel following a visit to the White Horse Tavern in Greenwich Village. Perhaps the most infamous event was the murder of Nancy Spungen, possibly by her boyfriend, Sex Pistols bass player Sid Vicious.

beats.script_body: The triangular sliver of land formed by the intersection of Fifth Avenue, Broadway, and 23rd Street dictated the foundation for this oddly shaped structure, completed in 1902. Designed by Daniel H. Burnham and Co., of Chicago World's Fair fame, and originally named the Fuller Building, this early skyscraper's three-sided configuration led to its current name. A National Historic Landmark, it was one of the first structures built with a steel frame that formed a strong foundation for its exterior walls — a principle employed in many later skyscrapers.

beats.script_body: This tree-lined neighborhood of architectural beauty was a swamp before it was laid out as one of New York's most attractive residential areas in 1822. The stretch of 19th Street between Irving Place and Third Avenue, with its many mid-19th-century town houses, was dubbed the "Block Beautiful." It was once home to artists and writers, including the journalist Ida Tarbell.

beats.script_body: The verdant ground stretching from 23rd to 26th Streets between Madison and Fifth Avenues has been a dedicated public space since 1686. The six-acre park has a significant role in baseball's history: the city's first team, the New York Knickerbockers, formed here in 1845, before it opened as Madison Square Park two years later. Today, benches sit among shady trees, historic statuary, and year-round public art.

beats.script_body: Financier Pierpont Morgan amassed an extraordinary collection of rare artwork, literature, and music memorabilia. Among its treasures are illuminated medieval and Renaissance manuscripts, a signed manuscript of a Mozart symphony, and the only surviving manuscript of Milton's Paradise Lost. Charles Dickens's manuscript of A Christmas Carol is always on view around Christmas, while permanent displays include Ancient Mesopotamian tablets and seals from 3000 B.C. onward.

beats.script_body: In 1924, after the financier's death, his son J. P. Morgan, Jr., gave the library to the public. Housed in a 1906 Renaissance-style villa designed by Charles McKim, it has a rotunda with an ornately decorated ceiling and inlaid marble floor. The Morgan campus also includes a light-filled courtyard by the noted Italian architect Renzo Piano, which connects the library's three main buildings.

beats.script_body: A massive temple to all things literary, the Stephen A. Schwarzman Building — better known as the main branch of the New York Public Library — opened in 1911. As well as housing 8.7 million treasured artifacts and books, the library has one of the world's longest and most famous reading rooms, loved by writers such as Norman Mailer and Alfred Kazin. The beaux arts building, designed by architects Carrère and Hastings, was designated a National Historic Landmark in 1965.

beats.script_body: Taking pride of place in the library's Rare Book Division is a Gutenberg Bible, printed around 1455. German publisher Johannes Gutenberg invented the printing press around 1440; some 180 Gutenberg Bibles were originally produced, yet only 48 survive. The story goes that when this rare tome arrived from Europe, New York Customs House officials were required to remove their hats in honor of the holy book.

review_queue.recommendation: Keep the historical/collection beats (Himalayan first-and-largest, Shiva mask) but mark the Rubin POI as physically closed so the tour does not route a listener to a shuttered building, or demote to walk_by_only. Do NOT delete the stories (never-auto-resolve: story deletion).

review_queue.description: OCR typo correction: book reads 'the only serving manuscript of Milton's Paradise Lost' — 'serving' is an OCR misread of 'surviving'. Beat script_body corrected to 'only surviving manuscript'. Confirmed against the Morgan's own catalog (themorgan.org) which describes it as the only surviving manuscript fragment used to print Paradise Lost. Single-source-class (publisher self-description) but a pure OCR fix, not a factual change.
review_queue.recommendation: Accept the OCR correction; no factual claim altered.
